analysis.one_liner: Caps wholesale electricity prices in the Western US and forces refunds of overcharges.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a vote as the 106th Congress ended in January 2001, with San Diego-area electricity bills still far above pre-spike levels.
analysis.plain_summary: During the summer of 2000, electricity prices in San Diego roughly doubled after the state's deregulated market left wholesale sellers free to charge what the market would bear. This bill would have ordered federal regulators to roll back Western wholesale electricity prices to their pre-spike level, required sellers to refund everything charged above that ceiling, and passed those refunds down to households and businesses. Sellers who violated the cap would owe triple the amount involved.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and small businesses in San Diego and across the Western grid who were paying sharply elevated electricity rates would get their overcharges refunded and see a ceiling return on future prices. Utilities and municipal power buyers who resell to consumers would pass the refunds through to the people who actually paid the inflated rates.
analysis.who_benefits_short: San Diego-area households and electricity customers

how_it_helps.text: Requires federal regulators to set a maximum wholesale electricity price in the Western System Coordinating Council, using the lower of the pre-spike three-year average price or a cost-based rate under the Federal Power Act.
Requires any seller who charged more than the maximum to refund the full excess, with the refund passed down the chain of purchasers until it reaches the ultimate consumers of the electricity.
Imposes civil penalties worth three times the value of any violation, to be assessed by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission after notice and a public hearing.

analysis.who_pays: Wholesale electricity sellers — including out-of-state power marketers and generators selling into the California market — would give back everything they charged above the pre-spike price ceiling and face triple-damages penalties for further violations.

drawbacks.text: A hard price ceiling set below market rates can discourage investment in new power plants and discourage sellers from supplying a strained market, which critics warned could worsen shortages during a supply crunch.
Retroactive refunds reach back to June 1, 2000, imposing a large one-time liability on sellers, some of whom argued their prices reflected genuine fuel and scarcity costs rather than excess profits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For San Diego customers facing bills that had jumped sharply in a single summer, the refund-and-cap approach offered direct, immediate relief, and the treble-damages provision gave the cap teeth. The main honest tradeoff is that a price ceiling imposed in a shortage can chill supply investment, which is why the price crisis was ultimately addressed through a mix of temporary federal price limits and longer-term market fixes rather than a permanent rollback. The bill never got a hearing, so its design was never tested or refined.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Commerce Committee and then to its Energy and Power Subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended in January 2001 with no hearing, no vote, and no further action.

narrative.text: Rep. Bob Filner introduced the bill on September 7, 2000, during the height of the San Diego electricity price spike.
The House referred it to the Committee on Commerce the day it was introduced.
Twelve days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power, and no further action is recorded.
The bill's only recorded support was its sponsor and two Republican cosponsors; the House never considered it, and the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wholesale electricity sellers kept the elevated revenues they had collected since June 2000 without any federal refund obligation, and the committee system that let the bill expire without a vote meant no member ever had to go on record on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wholesale power sellers kept their overcharges

for.name: Rep. Bob Filner
for.role: Sponsor; Representative for San Diego-area district
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the House floor after San Diego electricity prices spiked.

for.name: 2 House Republican cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the price-cap and refund bill.

against.name: House Committee on Commerce
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction; chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral, sent it to its Energy and Power Subcommittee, and never reported it out or scheduled any action before the Congress ended.

against.name: Western wholesale power generators and marketers
against.role: Sellers into the California and Western electricity markets
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal wholesale price caps and refund orders during the Western power crisis, arguing prices reflected scarcity and fuel costs.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor was a Democrat and both of its cosponsors were Republicans, but with only three supporters total and no floor action, no partisan voting pattern exists in the record.

industries.industry: Wholesale electricity sellers (generators and power marketers)
industries.note: The bill would force them to refund all revenue collected above the pre-June 2000 price level and face triple-damages penalties for future violations. Their gain from unregulated market pricing came directly out of San Diego households' electricity bills.

industries.industry: Retail electric utilities serving California customers
industries.note: Utilities that bought at wholesale and resold to consumers would be required to pass refunds through to their customers rather than keep them, which lowers their liability but reduces their revenue pool. Their customers would get the money back.
